newsitem.title: USA: House, Senate vote to cap U.S. ag export subsidies.
newsitem.headline: House, Senate vote to cap U.S. ag export subsidies.

text.p: The U.S. House and Senate passed fiscal 1998 agriculture appropriations bills on Thursday that sharply limit export subsidy spending despite signs the United States may soon begin discount grain sales.
In the House, lawmakers rejected proposals to reduce the peanut support price or alter the sugar loan program despite arguments the new "Freedom to Farm" law did not bring enough reform to them.
Both chambers, by narrow margins, turned down proposals to ban federally subsidized crop insurance for tobacco. They also defeated attempts to put more money into antismoking programs.

In its bill, the House voted to limit the Export Enhancement Program, the major U.S. ag export subsidy scheme, to $205 million. The Senate earmarked $150 million. The White House requested $500 million for EEP but did not elevate it to a make-or-break issue.

Agriculture Department officials say conditions in the coming year may warrant use of EEP. The administration was nearing a decision whether to offer cut-rate prices on wheat flour and malt barley. The United States has not subsidized grain sales for two years.
U.S. officials say action on export subsidies will depend on market conditions and behavior of competitors. They will closely monitor European Union prices.

Although the House and Senate trimmed EEP, each provided the maximum $5.7 billion for export credit guarantees, rejected any reduction in the $90 million a year cost-sharing Market Access Program to develop foreign markets and kept funding at current levels for the PL-480 Food for Peace program for food sales and humanitarian donations.
When House and Senate negotiators meet to write a compromise version of the bill, they will have to set a funding level for EEP. At least two other issues will need resolution:

--$91 million in prescription drug user fees for the Food and Drug Administration. On a point of order, the House struck authority for the fees from its bill. The Senate included them. Congress was working on separate legislation to reauthorize the fees.

--Crop insurance sales commissions. The Senate provided up to $200 million for commissions. The House provided $188 million for commissions, $36 million more than the White Housse requested. The Senate would allow commissions of 28 percent, the House slightly less. The administration suggested 24.5 percent.

Overall, the Senate alloted $50.7 billion for the Agriculture Department and related agencies. The House approved $49.5 billion. Funding this year was $53.9 billion. Public feeding programs, such as food stamps and school lunches, would get three-fourths of the fiscal 1998 funds.
